summary: Johann Dietrich Ludwig de Vries specialized in Indology and linguistics. He studied at Utrecht University under Willem Caland and Jos. Schrijnen, Amsterdam, Lille, and Bonn under Hermann Jacobi and Willibald Kirfel. In 1923, he was deputy Professor of Latin at Stellenbosch University.

Johann Friedrich Blumenbach worked in history, archaeology, and other fields. He studied at Ernestinum Gotha, the University of Jena (~1769–1772), and the University of Göttingen (~1772–1775), where he held a post from around 1776 to 1840.
Johann Friedrich Herbart was a philosopher who studied at the University of Jena (~1794–1797). He held a post at the University of Göttingen (~1805–1809) and taught Eduard Röer.

Johann Friedrich Kleuker worked in religious studies and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied at the University of Göttingen in 1770 and was appointed Professor of Theology at Kiel University in 1798. He taught Justus Olshausen.

Johann Gildemeister studied Indology and linguistics at Göttingen under Heinrich Ewald and Bonn under Georg Freytag, Christian Lassen, and A. W. von Schlegel. He taught at Bonn (PD 1839, Professor 1844–1889) and Marburg (Professor 1845, 1848–1858).

Johann Gottfried Eichhorn worked in religious studies, history, archaeology, and linguistics. He studied at Göttingen under Christian Gottlob Heyne (~1770–1774). He served as Professor at Jena (1775) and Göttingen (1788), and taught Franz Bopp and Heinrich Ewald.

Johann Gottfried Ludwig Kosegarten worked in Indology and linguistics. He studied at Greifswald and in Paris under Silvestre de Sacy and Chézy. He served as professor at the University of Jena (1817–1824) and the University of Greifswald (1824–1850).

Johann Gottfried von Herder worked in philosophy, linguistics, and religious studies. He studied under Immanuel Kant at the University of Königsberg. He held posts in Riga, as General Superintendent in Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach (1776), and as director of Wilhelm-Ernst-Gymnasium Weimar (~1776–1803).

Johann Gottlieb Rhode worked in Indology and religious studies. He studied at the University of Helmstedt (~1781–1785) and the University of Jena (~1820–1821). In 1809, he held a teaching post at the Kriegsschule Berlin.

Johann Gustav Stickel worked in linguistics. He studied at the University of Jena, under Johann Gottfried Ludwig Kosegarten, Andreas Gottlieb Hoffmann, and Antoine-Isaac Silvestre de Sacy. He served as a professor at the University of Jena from 1830 to 1836.

Johann Heinrich Kalthoff worked in Indology. He studied at Münster, Bonn, and under Silvestre de Sacy and Abel-Rémusat. He served as Privatdozent for Oriental languages and antiquities at the University of Münster (1830–1839) and taught French at Gymnasium Paulinum (1831).

Johann II Bernoulli studied at the University of Basel from approximately 1723 to 1729. He later held an academic post at the University of Basel from around 1736 to 1790 and taught Johann III Bernoulli.

Johann III Bernoulli was a scholar in Indology, history, archaeology, and other fields. He studied at Basel under Johann II and Daniel Bernoulli, and at Neuchâtel. He served as Royal Astronomer at Berlin Observatory and Director of the Prussian Academy of Sciences.
Johann Jakob Engel was a philosopher who studied at the University of Rostock (~1757–1761) and the University of Leipzig (~1762–1765). He taught Wilhelm von Humboldt.

Johann Jakob Meyer was an Indologist who studied at Concordia Senior College, Concordia Seminary, and the University of Chicago under Carl Darling Buck. He later served as a Docent at the University of Chicago from 1908 to 1919.

Johann Kirste worked in Indology and linguistics. He studied at Graz, Berlin, Jena, Vienna, Leipzig, and Paris under scholars including Georg Bühler and Albrecht Weber. He held posts at Vienna and Graz, becoming ordinary professor of Oriental philology at Graz in 1902.

Johann Peter Rottler was an Indologist and linguist who studied at the University of Strasbourg (~1770–1775). He served in the Danish-Halle Mission (~1776–1817), Vepery Mission (1817), Female Orphan Asylum (1808), and superintendent of Tranquebar Botanical Garden.

Johann Philipp Fabricius worked in linguistics and Indology. He studied law at the University of Giessen (~1732–1735) and theology at the University of Halle (~1735–1739), later succeeding Benjamin Schultze in 1742.

Johann Reinhold Forster studied at Joachimsthalsches Gymnasium, the University of Halle (~1748–1751), and Martin Luther University of Halle-Wittenberg. He held posts at Halle-Wittenberg (~1779–1798) and became Professor of Natural History at the University of Halle in 1780.

Johann Tobias Beck was a scholar in religious studies who studied at the University of Tübingen (~1822–1826). He later held academic posts at the University of Basel (~1836–1843) and the University of Tübingen (~1843–1878).
